sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Syn** (*syn*) ​— Refusal, Defense ‌· Refusal, ‌denial — is ​an ásynja of ​the Norse pantheon, ​the eleventh ​goddess in Snorri's ​catalogue of the ‌ásynjur: the doorkeeper ​who guards ​the door of ‌the hall and ​shuts it against ‌those who should ​not enter, ‌and the defender ​appointed at assemblies ​against the suits ​she wishes ​to refute — ​the power, in ‌short, of the ​word 'no'.[^1] ‌Her name is ​the common noun ‌itself: Old Norse ​*syn*, 'denial, ‌refusal', beside the ​verb *synja*, 'to ‌deny, refuse', and ​Snorri seals ​the identity with ‌the proverb he ‌records — 'a ‌denial is set ​up when ​a man says ‌no'.[^1][^2]

She has ​no surviving myth: ​no journey, ‌no marriage, no ​death. Her entire ​dossier is one ‌sentence of ​Gylfaginning, a name ‌in the ásynja ​þulur, and a ​place among ​the goddesses by ​whose names the ‌skalds may periphrase ‌a woman ​— and the ‌handbooks accordingly class ​her among the ​personified functions of ‌the catalogue, ‌an abstraction made ‌divine or a ‌faded minor deity ​surviving only ‌as an entry ​in the list.[^3]

​PuniCodex restores the ​name as ‌**Syn** — identical ​to the ASCII ​input, because normalized ​Old Norse ‌writes no diacritic ​in this name. ​The mechanical rule ​therefore places ‌the name in ​Tier 2: nothing ‌distinctive is lost ​in transit, a ‌statement about ​orthography and never ‌about the goddess. ‌The temple is ​domain-less: the ​plain-ASCII syn.com is ​registered to a ​third party outside ‌the collection ‌and is watched ​for release.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 35, ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. syn, synja.

Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Syn; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Syn.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Old Norse ‌as **Syn** — ​and it ​is not a ​theonym with a ​hidden etymology ​but the ordinary ‌noun itself. Old ​Norse *syn* ​(f.) means 'denial, ‌refusal'; the verb ​*synja* means ‌'to deny, to ​refuse', and it ‌saturates the ​legal prose of ​the sagas ​and the laws ​wherever a claim ​is answered ‌with a no.[^1] ​The etymological handbooks ‌connect the ​word with the ‌family of *sannr*, ​'true, sooth' ‌— a law ​term by origin: ‌the denial ​is the truth-speaking ​by which a ‌false accusation ‌is refused. The ‌goddess of ​saying no is, ​at root, the ‌goddess of ​the truthful answer.[^2]

​The ASCII form ‌is not ​a fallback here ​but the form ‌itself: normalized ​Old Norse writes ‌three plain Latin ​letters and ​a capital. Old ​Norse *y* is ​a rounded ‌front vowel unknown ‌to English, but ​the alphabet ‌writes it with ​an ordinary ​letter, so the ‌Unicode restoration **Syn** ‌preserves nothing ‌the ASCII alphabet ‌loses, and the ​mechanical rule ‌classifies the name ​Tier 2 — ​an orthographic ​fact, not a ‌judgment on the ​goddess.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation runs:

​- **s** → ‌**S** — ​Same, capitalized
- ​**y** → ​**y** — Same
‌- **n** → ​**n** — ‌Same

The project ​holds no domain ‌for this ​name. The plain-ASCII ‌**syn.com** is registered ‌to a ​third party outside ​the collection and ​is watched ​for release; this ‌temple claims nothing ‌it does ​not hold.[^3]

sources.citation: Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. syn, synja; Zoëga, Geir T., A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. syn, synja.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. syn, synja, sannr.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is ‌**/ˈsyn/** — Old ​Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

​- **S-** — ​Voiceless alveolar fricative ​[s], plain and ‌unaspirated, as ​in English 'say'
​- **-y-** — ‌Short close front ​rounded vowel ‌[y]: the tongue ​arched forward as ‌for English ​'ee' while the ​lips stay rounded ​as for 'oo' ​— the ​vowel of French ‌*tu* and German ​*über*
- **-n** ‌— Voiced ​alveolar nasal [n], ‌closing the single ​syllable cleanly

For ‌the modern ​speaker, the closest ‌approximation is: 'SUEN' ​with rounded ​lips — say ‌English 'seen' but ‌keep the lips ‌pursed from ​start to finish, ​so the vowel ‌comes out ​like French 'su'; ​one short syllable.

‌Kindred and historical ​forms of ​the name:

- ‌**Old Norse** — ​Syn, the goddess's ‌name; beside ​the noun syn, ​'denial, refusal', and ​the verb ​synja, 'to deny, ‌refuse'
- **Younger ‌Futhark** — ᛋᚢᚾ ​(s-u-n), the ‌Viking-Age runic rendering; ​the úr rune ​ᚢ covers y ‌along with ‌every rounded vowel[^2]
‌- **The proverb** ‌— 'syn er ​fyrir sett, ‌þá er maðr ​segir nei': a ​denial is ​set up when ‌a man says ​no
- **Modern ​Icelandic** — ​synja, 'to deny, ‌refuse', the living ​verb

Syn ​is Tier 2 ​because the restoration ‌preserves nothing the ​ASCII form ‌loses: no diacritic, ​no distinctive letter. ‌The stress falls ​on the ‌single syllable, as ‌it must; the ​y is ​short, and its ​rounded quality is ​the one articulatory ‌event the ‌plain spelling does ​not record.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (1957), runic appendix; Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (1957), s.v. syn.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name ​is preserved ‌in medieval Icelandic ‌manuscripts in ​the Latin alphabet ​as **Syn** ​— Old Norse ​(North Germanic), ​attested 13th c. ‌CE in ​the Codex Regius ​and Codex ‌Wormianus of the ​Prose Edda ‌and related codices, ​recording a ‌figure the tradition ​carried in ​a proverb.[^1] Before ​the Latin ​bookhand, Old Norse ​names were ‌carved in the ​Younger Futhark; ‌no runic attestation ​of this ‌theonym survives, so ​the manuscript ‌form is the ​primary witness. ‌The runic rendering ​is **ᛋᚢᚾ** ​(s-u-n).

The scholarly ‌rendering proceeds ‌step by step:

‌- The ​name is a ​simplex, not ‌a compound: three ​letters, one ​syllable, the short ‌rounded vowel ​y at its ​heart.
- ‌Old Norse orthography ​needs no ‌diacritic here: y ​is a ​plain letter, and ​no distinctive ​letter (þ, ð, ‌æ, ǫ) ‌occurs in the ​name.
- ‌In the Younger ​Futhark, the ​úr rune ᚢ ‌covers y ‌along with every ‌rounded vowel, ‌so the runic ​transliteration reads ‌'sun' — the ​one place ​the name's defining ​vowel disappears.
‌- The Unicode ​restoration Syn ​is therefore identical ​to the ‌ASCII form — ​the restoration ​is a matter ​of canonical ‌reference, not rescued ​orthography.
- ‌The name's identity ​with the ‌common noun *syn*, ​'denial, refusal', ‌and its kinship ‌with the ​family of *sannr*, ​'true', are ​registered in the ​lexica, and ‌are the whole ‌of the ​name's etymology.[^2]

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957).

de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. syn, synja; Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. syn.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Syn** is ​catalogued under ‌Refusal, Defense — ‌and the pairing ​is Snorri's ​own, for his ​single sentence ​gives her exactly ​two functions, at ‌the threshold ​and at the ​law-court, and ‌both are one ​function twice: ‌keeping the wrong ​thing out.[^1]

### ‌Refusal

Her ​name is the ​noun *syn*, ​'denial, refusal', and ​Snorri appends the ​proverb that ‌proves the word ​lived in ‌the language's mouth: ​a denial is ‌set up ​when a man ‌says no. ​She is the ‌only power in ​the Norse ​catalogue whose whole ‌office is ‌negative — the ‌divine right ​of refusal itself.[^1]

​### Defense

At ‌the þing, ​the assembly, she ​is appointed ‌to defend the ​suits she wishes ​to refute ‌— the lawful ​no, the ‌answer that stands ​between an accused ​person and ​a false claim. ​The word ‌is a law ‌term, kin to ​the family ‌of *sannr*, 'true': ​her defense ​is testimony, not ‌stubbornness.[^1]

### ‌The Door

She ‌guards the door ‌of the ​hall and shuts ‌it against ​those who should ​not enter. A ​household is ‌not safe because ​its doors ​are beautiful but ​because someone holds ‌them shut; ​Syn is that ​someone, made ​divine.[^1]

### The ‌Eleventh Seat

Snorri ​counts her ‌eleventh among the ​ásynjur, between ‌Vör and Hlín, ​and closes ‌the catalogue by ‌declaring these goddesses ​of no ​lesser rank than ​the rest ​— standing among ‌the goddesses for ‌one attested, ​indispensable function.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 35, trans. Faulkes (1987); on the word's legal sense, de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Brill, 1962), s.v. synja.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography of ‌Syn is ‌verbal rather ​than cultic ​— the ​corpus gives ​her no ​temple regalia, ‌no image, ​no attribute ​beyond the ‌two things ​her sentence ‌fixes, and ​what the ‌tradition remembered ​around them:[^1]

​- **The ​hall door** ​— the ​threshold she ‌holds ​against those ‌who should ​not enter: ‌the boundary ​made personal
‌- **The ​denial (syn)** ‌— the ​noun itself, ​the word ‌that says ‌no: refusal ‌elevated to ​a divine ​power
- ‌**The proverb** ​— 'a ​denial is ‌set up ​when a ​man says ‌no': ​the goddess ‌remembered in ​everyday speech, ​her mythology ​carried in ​a saying[^1]
‌- **The ‌seat among ​the ásynjur** ‌— eleventh ​in Snorri's ​catalogue, of ‌no lesser ‌rank: standing ‌among the ‌goddesses for ​a single ‌function[^1]
- ​**The defense ​at the ​þing** — ‌the ​legal shield: ​the right ​to answer ‌an accusation ​with a ​truthful no[^1]

​Beyond these, ‌the poets' ​craft keeps ‌one further ​emblem: her ‌name in ​the list ‌of ásynjur ‌by which ​a woman ​may be ​periphrased — ​refusal lending ‌her name ‌to the ​kenning.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 35, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (kennings for woman; ásynja þulur), trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Viking Society for Northern Research, 1998).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Syn's mythology is ​one sentence in Snorri, ‌one name in the þulur, ‌and one rule in the ​poets' grammar — the ​shortest dossier in the Edda, ​carried in a proverb.

### ​The Eleventh Ásynja (Gylfaginning ​35)

Snorri's catalogue of the ‌goddesses moves from [[frigg|Frigg]] through ​[[saga|Sága]], [[eir|Eir]], [[gefjon|Gefjon]], [[fulla|Fulla]], ​[[freyja|Freyja]] and the rest, and ‌arrives at the eleventh: ​Syn. 'She guards the door ‌of the hall and shuts ​it against those who ‌should not enter, and she ​is appointed to defend, at ​assemblies, the suits she ​wishes to refute.' Then the ​sentence that fixes her identity: ​'hence the proverb that ‌a denial is set up ​when a man says ‌no.' The catalogue closes with ​Snotra and Gná, and Snorri ‌adds that these ásynjur ​are of no lesser rank ‌than the rest.[^1]

### The ​Word Made Goddess (Gylfaginning ‌35)

Snorri knows exactly what ​he is doing when he ​appends the proverb: he ‌is recording a figure the ‌language itself had already ‌made. Old Norse *syn* means ​'denial, refusal', and the verb ​*synja* does its ordinary ‌work in the law-cases of ​the sagas wherever a claim ​is refused. Whether Syn ‌was an old goddess whose ​function shrank to a saying, ​or an abstraction the ‌cataloguing mind personified on the ​model of Vör, Hlín ‌and Snotra, the handbooks will ​not decide; Simek and Lindow ​class her among the ​personified functions, and the evidence ​is too thin to overrule ‌them.[^2]

### The Kenning ‌for a Woman (Skáldskaparmál)

Skáldskaparmál's ​rules for the poets keep ‌Syn in the craft ​of verse: a woman may ​be periphrased by the ‌name of any ásynja, and ‌Syn stands in the list ‌— refusal lending her ‌name to praise. The ásynja ​þulur, the versified name-lists preserved ‌with the same section ​of the Edda, hold her ​in the catalogue by name: ​every skald who named ‌a woman after an ásynja ​worked from a list ​that included her.[^3]

### The ​Silence of the Poems

No ‌eddic poem names Syn. ​Völuspá does not number her ​among the returning gods; Grímnismál's ​survey of heaven's halls ‌gives her no dwelling. Where ​[[nanna|Nanna]] at least has her ‌household's hall in verse, ​Syn has only the sentence ‌— and the saying. ​The silence is itself the ‌evidence the handbooks weigh: a ‌figure attested once, in ​a catalogue, beside a living ​proverb, is either a genuine ​minor cult figure the ​poems happened to miss or ‌a personification promoted from grammar. ‌The honest record keeps ​both doors open.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 35, trans. Faulkes (1987).

Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Syn; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Syn.
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (kennings for woman) and ásynja þulur, trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Viking Society for Northern Research, 1998).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Syn's nearest ​kin are ‌inside her own ‌catalogue: the ​company of ásynjur ​whom Snorri ​lists around her ​— Vör, ​'awareness', who ‌is wise and ​searching so ​that nothing can ‌be hidden ​from her; Hlín, ‌set to ​guard those whom ‌Frigg wishes ​to save from ​danger; Snotra, ​wise and courteous; ​Gná, whom ​Frigg sends on ‌errands through ​the worlds. ‌Simek and Lindow ​treat this ‌whole band, Syn ​among them, ‌as personified functions ​and abstractions ‌— the grammatically ​feminine nouns ​of Old Norse ‌promoted to ‌goddesses, or faded ‌minor deities ​surviving only as ​entries in ‌the list.[^1]

​The comparison most ​often drawn ‌is structural, not ​borrowed. The ​doorkeeper type recurs ‌across the ​North — the ‌corpus's own ​great threshold-guardian is ​Heimdallr at ​Bifröst — but ​where Heimdallr ‌watches for ‌what comes, Syn ​simply refuses ‌it entry. Nineteenth-century ​scholars reached ​further, to the ‌door-keeping figures ‌of other traditions, ‌even Janus ‌with his gates; ​the modern ‌handbooks are cooler, ​and note ​that nothing beyond ​the single ‌sentence supports ​reconstruction.[^2] What can ​be said ​cleanly is that ‌no other ​northern goddess is ​so entirely ​a speech-act — ‌a goddess ​whose whole cult, ‌if she ​ever had one, ‌fits in ​the space of ‌the word ‌'no'. Within ​the corpus, her ​related figures ​are the catalogue ​that holds ‌her: [[frigg|Frigg]], [[fulla|Fulla]], ‌[[saga|Sága]], [[eir|Eir]], ​and [[gefjon|Gefjon]].

sources.citation: Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Syn, Vör, Hlín, Gná; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Syn.
Orchard, Andy, Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend (London: Cassell, 1997), s.v. Syn, Heimdall.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Syn's ​afterlife is ‌the quietest ‌in the ​pantheon and ​the most ​grammatical. The ​proverb Snorri ​recorded — ‌a denial ​is set ​up when ‌a man ​says no ‌— remained ​in circulation ‌as a ​saying about ​plain ​refusal, and ​the verb ​*synja* never ‌died: it ​lives on ‌in modern ​Icelandic and ‌Faroese as ​the ordinary ‌word for ​denying and ‌refusing, so ​that the ​goddess's name ‌is still ‌spoken daily ‌by ​people who ​have never ‌heard of ​her.[^1]

The ​handbooks of ‌Norse mythology ​keep her ​one-sentence entry ‌with bureaucratic ​fidelity: Simek, ‌Orchard and ​Lindow all ​give her ​a short ​article, always ‌the same ‌two functions, ​always ‌the same ​scholarly shrug ​about personification.[^2] ‌Modern Heathen ‌and Ásatrú ‌communities, working ‌through the ​ásynjur name ‌by name, ​have found ​in her ​a goddess ‌worth invoking ​for the ​age of ​obligations: the ‌patron ​of boundaries, ​of the ​lawful refusal, ‌of the ​strength to ‌say no ​at the ‌door and ​at the ‌judgment-seat — ‌a modern ​devotion built ​honestly on ​the only ​two functions ‌the sources ‌ever gave ​her.

sources.citation: Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. synja.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Syn.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
Syn ​is a ‌wholly textual ‌goddess: no ​runestone invokes ​her, ​no place-name ​preserves her, ​no votive ‌deposit names ​her, ​and no ‌image can ​be identified ‌with her ​— ‌a silence ​she shares ​with most ​of the ​minor ​ásynjur of ‌Snorri's catalogue ​and one ‌that ​underwrites the ‌scholarly reading ​of her ‌as a ​personified ‌function rather ​than an ​independently culted ‌deity.[^1]

Her ‌attestation ‌hangs on ​the manuscript ​witnesses of ‌Snorri's Edda: ​the ​Codex Regius ‌and Codex ​Wormianus for ​Gylfaginning 35, ‌and ​the manuscripts ‌of Skáldskaparmál ​— the ​Codex Regius ​and ​AM 748 ‌among them ‌— for ​the kenning ‌rule ​and the ​ásynja þulur ‌that keep ‌her name ‌in ‌the register ​of the ‌goddesses.[^2] The ​nearest material ​context ​is the ‌word itself: ​the legal ​prose ​of the ‌medieval Icelandic ​laws and ​sagas, where ​synja ‌does its ​ordinary work ‌of refusing ​claims, is ‌the ​closest thing ‌the record ‌offers to ​a cult ​site ​— the ​door and ‌the þing, ‌preserved on ​vellum.

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Syn.
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, ed. Anthony Faulkes (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1982–98), on the manuscript tradition of Gylfaginning and the þulur.

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
The ​Poetic Edda ‌never stages ‌Syn: no ​surviving eddic ​poem names ​her, gives ​her a ​line, or ‌numbers her ​among the ​gods. Völuspá's ‌seeress, who ​foretells the ‌return of ​Baldr ‌and [[hodr|Höðr]] ​after Ragnarǫk, ​does not ​name her ​among the ​returning; Grímnismál's ‌numbered survey ​of heaven's ‌dwellings gives ​her no ‌hall.[^1] Where ​[[nanna|Nanna]] at ‌least has ​her ‌household's Glitnir ​held in ​verse independent ‌of Snorri, ‌Syn's whole ‌being rests ​on the ​prose catalogue, ‌the þulur, ​and the ​noun the ‌whole language ​spoke.

What ​the eddic ‌corpus ​does supply ‌is the ​genre that ​preserved her: ​the þulur ​— versified ‌catalogues of ‌names, of ​which Völuspá's ‌dwarf-list is ​the famous ​example — ‌are the ‌native form ‌of ‌the name-register ​in which ‌the ásynja ​lists, appended ​to Skáldskaparmál, ​keep Syn ‌among the ​goddesses.[^1] The ​silence of ​the mythological ‌lays themselves ​remains the ​sharpest fact ​about ‌her: a ​figure attested ‌once, in ​a catalogue, ‌beside a ​living proverb, ‌is either ‌a minor ​cult figure ​the poems ​happened to ​miss or ‌a personification ‌promoted from ​grammar.[^2]

sources.citation: The Poetic Edda, trans. Carolyne Larrington, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014) — the corpus's silence; the þulur form.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Syn.

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
The Prose ​Edda is ‌Syn's entire ‌witness, and it ​is one ​sentence long ​— but Snorri ​makes the ​sentence do ‌the work of ​a myth. ​Gylfaginning 35 ‌places her eleventh ​in the ‌catalogue of ​the ásynjur, after ‌[[frigg|Frigg]], [[saga|Sága]], ​[[eir|Eir]], [[gefjon|Gefjon]], ​[[fulla|Fulla]], [[freyja|Freyja]], Sjöfn, ​Lofn, Vár ​and Vör, ​and before Hlín, ‌Snotra and ​Gná: she ‌guards the door ​of the ‌hall against ​those who should ‌not enter, ​and she ‌is appointed to ​defend at ​assemblies the ‌suits she wishes ‌to refute. ‌Then comes ​the etymological flourish ​that is ‌pure Snorri: ​the proverb, 'a ​denial is ‌set up ​when a man ​says no', ‌appended so ​that the ‌reader sees the ​goddess and ​the grammar ​are one.[^1]

Snorri's ​craft deserves ‌note. The ‌catalogue is careful ​to rank ‌its figures ​— Fulla carries ​Frigg's casket ‌and wears ‌the golden band; ‌Gná rides ‌the sea ​and air on ‌Hófvarpnir — ​and then ​gives Syn the ​plainest entry ‌of all, ​two functions and ​a saying. ​The ásynja ‌þulur preserved with ​Skáldskaparmál hold ​her in ​the versified register ‌by name, ​and Skáldskaparmál's ‌kenning rules keep ​her available ‌to the ​poets as a ‌name by ‌which any ​woman may be ​periphrased: a ​deity of ​one sentence, kept ‌with bureaucratic ‌fidelity among ​the ásynjur.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 35, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (kennings for woman) and ásynja þulur, trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Viking Society for Northern Research, 1998).

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
The ​runic corpus ‌contains no ‌invocation ​of the ​goddess ​Syn. No ​runestone asks ​her ‌favour, no ​amulet bears ​her ‌name, and ​no ‌inscription yet ​found links ‌a ​dedicant to ​her cult ​— ​a silence ​she ‌shares with ​the whole ‌company ​of minor ‌ásynjur in ​Snorri's ‌catalogue and ​one ‌that marks ​her as ​a ‌literary-mythological figure ‌rather than ‌an ​independently culted ​deity.[^1]

‌What can ​be said ​runologically ‌is the ​rendering itself: ​in ‌the Younger ​Futhark ‌the name ​would have ​been ​carved ᛋᚢᚾ ​(s-u-n). The ‌sixteen-rune ‌row underspecifies ​the ‌vowel — ​the úr ​rune ‌ᚢ covers ‌/u, o, ‌ø, ‌ǫ, y/ ​and ‌/w/ — ​so the ​runic ​transliteration reads ‌'sun', and ​the ​rounded front ​vowel ‌y that ​defines the ​name ​in the ‌manuscripts is ​invisible ‌in the ​runes. ‌No Viking-Age ​carving of ‌the ‌theonym is ​known; the ​manuscript ​spelling of ​the ‌Edda remains ‌the primary ​witness.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Syn.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957), runic appendix.

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
Beyond the ​Eddas, Syn ‌has no ‌medieval afterlife ​as a ​person — ​no Saxo, ​no saga ​episode, no euhemerized ‌queen. What ​survives in ​the wider ‌medieval record ​is the ‌word she ​bears. The ‌noun *syn* and ​the verb ​*synja* saturate ​the legal ​prose of ​the sagas ‌and the ​Icelandic laws: ‌wherever a claim ​is refused, ‌a charge ​denied, an ‌offer declined ​at the ‌þing, her ​name does ​its ordinary work ‌as grammar. ‌The proverb ‌Snorri recorded ​— a ​denial is ‌set up ​when a ​man says no ‌— is ​the trace ​of that ‌everyday usage ​rising, for ‌one sentence, ​into theology.[^1]

​The poets' craft ​keeps the ​person as ‌well as ‌the word. ​Skáldskaparmál's rules ‌allow a ​woman to ​be periphrased by ‌the name ‌of any ‌ásynja, and ‌Syn stands ​in the ‌list the ​kenning-makers inherited ​— refusal lending ​her name ‌to praise ​in the ​same breath ​as [[freyja|Freyja]] ‌and [[fulla|Fulla]]. ​The ásynja ​þulur, copied into ​the manuscripts ‌of the ​Edda, preserved ‌her name ​in the ‌register of ​the goddesses ‌for the scribes ‌of the ​thirteenth and ​fourteenth centuries ​— the ​whole of ‌her saga, ‌told in ​a list.[^2]

sources.citation: Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. syn, synja.
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (kennings for woman) and ásynja þulur, trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Viking Society for Northern Research, 1998).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Syn is ​the pantheon's ‌smallest power ‌and perhaps ​its most ​modern one. ​Every other ​goddess in ​Snorri's catalogue ‌presides over ​something the world ​desires — ‌love, healing, ​wisdom, safe ‌passage, the ​keeping of ‌oaths. Syn ​presides over ​the thing ​everyone needs ​and no one ​thanks: the ‌refusal. The ​door that ‌does not ​open. The ‌claim that ​does not ‌stand. Hers ​is the only ‌divine function ​in the ​corpus that ‌is purely ‌negative, and ‌the tradition ​ranks her, ​deliberately, of ‌no lesser ​worth — a ​household is ‌not safe ​because its ​doors are ‌beautiful but ​because someone ‌holds them ​shut.[^1]

And ​there is ​a deeper point ​folded into ‌the etymology. ‌The word ​she bears ‌is a ​law term, ​kin to ‌the word ‌for truth: ‌the denial is ‌not stubbornness ​but testimony, ‌the truthful ​no that ​answers the ​false claim. ‌In a ​mythology that ​ends with the ​doors of ‌the world ​broken down ​at Ragnarǫk, ​Syn stands ‌at the ​threshold for ‌as long ​as the ‌hall stands — ​the goddess ‌of the ‌boundary, reminding ​us that ​a wall ​is only ​architecture until ‌someone is ‌willing to ​say no.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 35, trans. Faulkes (1987); de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Brill, 1962), s.v. synja.
